interviewQuestions.question: How would you run a rightsizing pass across a fleet without risking a performance regression?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start from utilization data, not guesswork — pull CPU and memory percentiles, specifically p95/p99 rather than average, over at least a few weeks to capture real peak behavior, since average utilization hides exactly the spikes that justify a resource's current sizing. Anything consistently running well under its request/limit even at p99 over that whole window is a genuine rightsizing candidate; anything whose p99 occasionally approaches its limit is not, even if its average looks low.

Concretely, I'd downsize incrementally and monitor rather than resize the whole fleet at once: change one instance class or one Kubernetes request/limit for a small batch, watch latency and error rate through a *full* traffic cycle including that batch's own peak — not just a quiet afternoon — and only proceed to the next batch once the first is confirmed safe over that full cycle. This staged approach catches the case where a resource looked oversized in the data but actually needed the extra room for a monthly batch job or an occasional retry storm that the sampling window happened to miss.

I'd specifically avoid a single fleet-wide resize based on a snapshot of last week's traffic, since that misses seasonal patterns (a service quiet in summer, busy in Q4) and growth trends (traffic climbing steadily means today's "safe" downsize is next month's incident). I'd also keep a fast rollback path — reverting a request/limit change is cheap, and having it ready means a staged rollout can move confidently instead of overly conservatively.

**Testing:** whether you rightsize from percentile data plus a staged rollout with real rollback, not from averages applied fleet-wide in one shot.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Running a safe rightsizing pass

interviewQuestions.question: What kinds of waste would you look for in a cloud bill beyond just oversized instances?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd widen the search past compute sizing to categories of waste that accumulate silently precisely because nothing ever alerts on them — an oversized instance shows up in a utilization dashboard, but an orphaned resource often doesn't show up anywhere until someone goes looking.

Orphaned resources are the biggest category: unattached EBS volumes left behind after an instance was terminated, load balancers still running after the service behind them was decommissioned, elastic IPs reserved but never attached to anything, all billing quietly with zero traffic or usage. A concrete, extremely common pattern: a team migrates a service off a VM to a new platform and deletes the instance, but the instance's attached disk survives the deletion by design (so data isn't lost accidentally) — and then nobody remembers to delete the disk itself, so it keeps billing indefinitely with nothing pointing at it.

Second, snapshots and backups retained indefinitely with no lifecycle policy — a daily snapshot schedule with no expiration accumulates linearly forever, and a team that set it up two years ago is now paying for 700+ snapshots when a 30-day retention policy would have covered every real recovery scenario they'd actually use.

Third, storage sitting on a premium, low-latency tier when the actual access pattern doesn't need it — logs or old backups on frequently-accessed-tier object storage that haven't been read in months belong on an infrequent-access or archive tier at a fraction of the cost.

I'd operationalize finding all of this with tagging discipline plus a scheduled automated audit — AWS Trusted Advisor, or a custom query against the billing API for resources with zero recent activity — rather than relying on someone remembering to manually clean up after every migration, since that discipline reliably breaks down under deadline pressure.

**Testing:** whether you think beyond "my instance is too big" to the orphaned-resource and storage-tiering waste that accumulates precisely because nothing alerts on it.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Finding waste beyond oversized compute

interviewQuestions.question: Why does rightsizing need to be an ongoing process instead of a one-time project?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The thing being sized — traffic, code, dependencies — keeps changing after the rightsizing pass ends, so a correct sizing today silently drifts wrong over months without anyone doing anything wrong. A service rightsized for its current traffic will be oversized again after a feature ships that reduces its computational work (a cache added, a slow query fixed), or undersized after organic growth, and in both directions nobody notices until either the bill flags waste or the latency graph flags risk — and by the time either of those fires, the drift has usually been accumulating for a while.

Concretely, a team that rightsizes once a year carries, on average, six-plus months of accumulated waste (or in the worse direction, six-plus months of accumulated risk) before the next scheduled pass would even look at it — and if growth was fast during that window, the "correct" sizing from a year ago might now be dangerously undersized well before the annual review catches it.

I'd instead build rightsizing into a recurring, largely automated cadence — monthly or quarterly reports on utilization drift per service, ideally flagged proactively rather than requiring someone to remember to run the report — so it's a standing operational check like patching or backup verification, not a one-off initiative that competes for attention with feature work and reliably loses. The teams that do this well usually tie it to an existing recurring ritual — a monthly cost review, a quarterly capacity planning meeting — rather than inventing a new standalone process that's easy to skip when things get busy.

**Testing:** whether you understand rightsizing as tracking a moving target that needs a recurring process, not a fix-once checkbox.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why a one-time rightsizing pass decays
